reviews.review_description: Georges Méliès queria ter sido pintor, mas o pai não apoiou a ideia. Antes de se tornar o grande cineasta que foi, trabalhou na fábrica da família e construiu carreira nos palcos, como mágico ilusionista. Esteve presente no Salon Indien du Grand Café, em 28 de dezembro de 1895, quando os Irmãos Lumière exibiram seus primeiros curtas. Ofereceu dez mil francos aos Lumière pelas câmeras do cinematógrafo, oferta de pronto recusada pela dupla (que já havia recusado ofertas bem maiores do Museu de Cera de Paris – Musée Grévin – e até do Folies Bergère). Não podendo ter o cinematógrafo, Méliès foi a Londres e comprou um Teatógrafo (ou Animatógrafo) de Robert William Paul, eletricista e fabricante britânico de aparelhos ópticos, que também se tornou cineasta; máquina semelhante ao da famosa dupla francesa. E com este aparelho, o mágico, o inventor e o frustrado pintor em Méliès ganhou asas e criou alguns dos mais divertidos, aterrorizantes e fantásticos sonhos que o Primeiro Cinema conheceu.

In this early silent film by director Georges Melies, we see a part of the start of cinema. An Astronomer (Victor Andre) studies the moon and builds a rocket. With his invention he assigns a Captain (Henri Delannoy) who leads his crew on a voyage to a mysterious land.

did_you_know_list.title: The theft Méliès suffered
did_you_know_list.description: After filming was over, Georges Méliès intended to release the film in the United States and profit from it. Unfortunately, Thomas A. Edison had already secretly made copies, and within a few weeks the film was already on American soil. Méliès never made any money from the success he had in the United States, and went bankrupt a few years later, while Edison made a fortune off the film.

did_you_know_list.title: A pioneering film
did_you_know_list.description: This was one of the earliest known science fiction films. A part near the end was animated, which also makes it one of the first animated films.

did_you_know_list.title: Discovery of a copy in 2002
did_you_know_list.description: In 2002, a copy of the film was discovered in a barn in France. The incredible thing was not only that most of the film was there, but also that it was entirely hand-colored. The film was restored and released the following year at the Pordenone Silent Film Festival.

block_special.description:
When we think about A Trip to the Moon, our minds are immediately taken over by the early, mythical idea that in its beginnings cinema was an art whose "rules" were established during the production process itself. This French film was released in 1902 and represented a revolution for its time, given its length (approximately 14 minutes) compared to the two-minute shorts that were being produced.

A Trip to the Moon directly reflects the theatrical personality of its director, Georges Méliès, whose past as a stage actor and magician influenced the production of the film. The work boldly experiments with some of the most famous cinematic techniques, such as superimpositions, dissolves and editing practices that would later be widely used. Despite the simplicity of its special effects, the film is considered the first example of science fiction cinema. It features many of the genre's characteristic elements - a spaceship, the discovery of a new frontier - and establishes most of its conventions.

Méliès's film deserves a prominent place among the icons of world film history. Despite its surreal style, A Trip to the Moon is fun and innovative, managing to combine theatrical tricks with the infinite possibilities of the film medium. Méliès was more of a maestro than a director, also working as screenwriter, actor, producer, set designer, costume designer and cinematographer, creating special effects that were considered spectacular at the time. This first science fiction film is a must-see for anyone interested in the origin of the conventions that later influenced the entire genre and its most famous entries. More generally, A Trip to the Moon can be considered the film that establishes the main distinction between fiction and nonfiction cinema. At a time when cinema mostly portrayed everyday life, as in the films of the Lumière brothers at the end of the 19th century, Méliès managed to offer a fantasy aimed at pure and simple entertainment. He opened the doors for the filmmakers of the future by visually expressing his creativity in a way completely foreign to the films of the time.
block_special.credits: Original analysis by Chiara Ferrari, adapted from the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

quote.quote: Méliès was truly a magician... He understood the possibilities of a motion picture camera.

block_special.description:
The Great Train Robbery is considered the first Western ever made, launching what would become, within a few years, the most popular film genre in the United States. Produced by the Edison Company in November 1903, it was the most commercially successful film of the pre-Griffith period of American cinema and spawned countless imitations.

What makes Edwin S. Porter's film exceptional is its degree of narrative sophistication, considering when it was made. There are more than a dozen distinct scenes, each one deepening the plot further.

One of the actors in The Great Train Robbery was G. M. Anderson (his real name was Max Aronson). Among other roles, he played the passenger who gets shot. Anderson would soon become the first Western star, appearing as Broncho Billy in more than 100 films starting in 1907.

Years later, some disputed the claim that The Great Train Robbery was the first Western ever made, arguing either that it was not the first or that it was not a Western. There were undoubtedly earlier films that used the theme, such as Cripple Creek Bar-Room Scene (1899), but they lack the narrative unity of Porter's film.

It can be said that its roots lie both in stage plays featuring spectacular railroad scenes and in other films about daring robberies that did not belong to the genre. Nor can it be argued that it is a true Western on the basis of authentic locations, since The Great Train Robbery was shot on the Delaware-Lackawanna railroad in New Jersey. Nevertheless, ever since the days of Jesse James, train robberies have been part of the mythology of this type of film, and other symbolic elements such as six-shooters, cowboy hats and horses give the film a genuine Western atmosphere.

did_you_know_list.title: An important step in filmmaking
did_you_know_list.description: The film uses simple editing techniques (each scene is a single take) and the story is quite linear, representing an important step in filmmaking. It is also one of the first "narrative" films.

did_you_know_list.title: Frightened audiences
did_you_know_list.description: The final scene in which the gun is fired at the camera had a profound effect on audiences. Since cinema was in its very early days, many people were frightened by the shot because they thought they would be hit.

did_you_know_list.title: The famous shot
did_you_know_list.description: The film was originally distributed with a note saying that the much-talked-about shot the bandit fires at the camera could be placed at either the beginning or the end of the film. It ended up staying at the end.

did_you_know_list.title: The film's negative in perfect condition
did_you_know_list.description: The film's negative still exists and is in excellent condition. The Library of Congress, which holds the negative, can still make new prints.

did_you_know_list.title: Tom London's first film
did_you_know_list.description: This is the first of 20 other appearances by actor Tom London, a veteran of Westerns. He was cast as the locomotive engineer, his real job at the time.

quote.quote: We consider it, in every respect, the best moving picture film ever made.
quote.author: Edison Company catalog

did_you_know_list.title: No Screenplay
did_you_know_list.description: Director D.W. Griffith visualized the entire film in his mind, without writing a screenplay or making notes about the scenes.

did_you_know_list.title: 100 minutes
did_you_know_list.description: It was the first film in history to run longer than 100 minutes.

did_you_know_list.title: An expensive film
did_you_know_list.description: It premiered in New York with tickets costing US$2 each, an astronomical sum for the time. Even so, the film stayed in theaters for a year and drew more than a million people.

did_you_know_list.title: Racist content
did_you_know_list.description: Because of its racist content, The Birth of a Nation was banned in several major US cities, such as Los Angeles.

quote.quote: It is the greatest thing I have achieved, but I will not be satisfied until I do something more... I am, like all human beings, driven by perfection.
quote.author: D. W. Griffith

did_you_know_list.title: No stunt doubles
did_you_know_list.description: Musidora was an acrobat, so she did all the scenes herself and did without stunt doubles.

did_you_know_list.title: Must see before you die
did_you_know_list.description: It is included in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die, edited by Steven Jay Schneider.

quote.quote: A film is not a sermon, nor a lecture... but a means of entertaining the eyes and the mind.
quote.author: Louis Feuillade

movies.title: Intolerance: Love's Struggle Throughout the Ages

did_you_know_list.title: The intolerance against Griffith
did_you_know_list.description: The inspiration for this film came when D.W. Griffith was taken aback by the protests against his previous film, The Birth of a Nation. In response to the attacks he had been facing, he wanted to show the problem of intolerance from several points of view.

did_you_know_list.title: The Wall of Hollywood
did_you_know_list.description: The Wall of Babylon was built at a size equivalent to the original just for the film, and it stood for a long time at the corner of Sunset Boulevard and Hollywood Boulevard, in California. It became a notable landmark during Hollywood's golden years. The replica was the first outdoor set ever built in Hollywood. Only after many years, when it had already deteriorated, was it torn down. Many years later, a replica of the replica was built at the Hollywood & Highland complex and unveiled in 2001.

did_you_know_list.title: Under the supervision of a rabbi
did_you_know_list.description: The wedding scenes in the life-of-Christ segment were shot according to Jewish tradition, under the supervision of Rabbi Myers. He was the father of Carmel Myers, who played a slave girl in the Babylon scenes.

did_you_know_list.title: 60 injured at the production hospital
did_you_know_list.description: During the filming of the battle sequence, many extras got so deeply into character that they hurt one another. At the end of one day, a total of 60 injured people were treated at the production's makeshift hospital.

did_you_know_list.title: Too few Romans
did_you_know_list.description: D.W. Griffith was forced to reshoot the crucifixion sequence because some organizations said Griffith had filmed too many Jewish extras around the cross and too few Romans. Griffith then heeded the complaint and put more Romans in the shot.

quote.quote: The fragrant mystery of your body is greater than the mystery of life.
quote.author: Intolerance, Intertitle

did_you_know_list.title: The first of its genre
did_you_know_list.description: It is considered by many to be the first horror film in history.

did_you_know_list.title: Fritz Lang considered as director
did_you_know_list.description: Producer Erich Pommer wanted Fritz Lang to direct. Lang was even interested, but decided to work on another film.

did_you_know_list.title: Another actress instead of Hans's girlfriend
did_you_know_list.description: Hans Janowitz wrote the female lead for his girlfriend Gilda Langer, a stage actress in Berlin, but it was Lil Dagover who got the role.

did_you_know_list.title: A film made of paper and paint
did_you_know_list.description: The sets were made of paper, and the shadows were painted on the walls.

quote.quote: Wiene treated costume as if it were decor. He even used something like plaster as makeup to suggest a ghost.
quote.author: David Thomson, critic

did_you_know_list.title: Filming at night
did_you_know_list.description: Filming took 18 days and nights. Donald Crisp's scenes were shot at night because he was directing another film during the day.

did_you_know_list.title: Griffith's purchase
did_you_know_list.description: The film was originally made for Adolph Zukor at Paramount Pictures. D.W. Griffith bought it so he could release it through his new company, United Artists.

did_you_know_list.title: Selected by the Library of Congress
did_you_know_list.description: The film was selected for the National Film Registry of the Library of Congress in 1996.

quote.quote: Her beauty, so long hidden, shines like a poem.
quote.author: Broken Blossoms, Intertitle

did_you_know_list.title: Lost for 70 years
did_you_know_list.description: The film was lost for more than 70 years and, after being found at the Filmoteca Española, it was restored.

did_you_know_list.title: Strong scenes
did_you_know_list.description: The film was edited several times because the rape and lynching scenes were considered too strong in light of the race riots that took place in Chicago in 1919.

did_you_know_list.title: The first "Black film"
did_you_know_list.description: This is one of the oldest known films made by an African American, and also with a predominantly Black cast.

quote.quote: I was deeply stirred by this film... I was moved by its enormous cinematic power.
quote.author: Ingmar Bergman

quote.quote: Next to this film, the ordinary screenplay becomes as thin and white as the paper it was printed on.
quote.author: The New York Times

did_you_know_list.title: Stoker's Dracula
did_you_know_list.description: Originally, Nosferatu was to be titled "Dracula", like the Bram Stoker book that inspired it. However, since Stoker himself did not authorize the use of the name, director Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau decided to change it to the current title.

did_you_know_list.title: A story never told before
did_you_know_list.description: Nosferatu is the first screen version of the classic story of Count Dracula.

did_you_know_list.title: The curse of the sun
did_you_know_list.description: The popular notion that sunlight kills vampires is based on this story. Nosferatu was the first film to show a vampire dying this way.

quote.quote: You can't leave now. The werewolf is roaming the forests.
quote.author: Nosferatu, Innkeeper

did_you_know_list.title: Without the help of historians
did_you_know_list.description: Director Benjamin Christensen originally planned to write the screenplay with the help of historians, but the plan went down the drain when he learned that most of the scholars he had in mind were against the film.

did_you_know_list.title: The film's "special effects"
did_you_know_list.description: To create the scene in which the witches fly over the town's rooftops, Benjamin Christensen and his cameraman Johan Ankerstjerne photographed a miniature town (each house was about 2 meters tall) in a huge model, all handmade, which took 20 men to complete. Then several actors in costume, mounted on brooms, were photographed against a black background. An airplane engine was needed to make their robes flutter in the wind. A total of 75 witches were photographed, each one individually, and then Johan built a special optical printer to put the witches together.

did_you_know_list.title: The gloomy atmosphere of the shoot
did_you_know_list.description: Although most of the film's scenes were shot in closed studios (because Benjamin believed the actors would perform better if they were influenced by a darker, gloomier atmosphere), the film also included exterior scenes. Most of these scenes were shot at night, which was unthinkable at the time.

quote.quote: We no longer burn our old and poor, but do they not still suffer cruelly?
quote.author: Häxan, Intertitle

quote.quote: Without organization of the masses, the proletariat is nothing. Organized, it is everything.
quote.author: Lenin, Intertitle

did_you_know_list.title: The controversy over the director
did_you_know_list.description: Some sources cite Roscoe "Fatty" Arbuckle as the film's co-director. Whether this is true is unknown. Buster Keaton originally wanted Arbuckle to work as co-director, but Arbuckle was still quite depressed over the scandal two years earlier that had nearly ruined his career, and he had become a difficult person to deal with. Doris Deane, Arbuckle's second wife, later said her husband had directed the entire film. However, there is controversy over how much he actually did.

did_you_know_list.title: The production of the film within the film
did_you_know_list.description: When Buster Keaton falls asleep while projecting a film, he dreams and a film within the film begins. We are then told that the film was produced by the "Veronal Film Company", a very fitting name since Veronal was the world's first sleeping pill.

did_you_know_list.title: Keaton's stunts
did_you_know_list.description: Buster Keaton, the actor-director often compared to Chaplin, performed all of the film's stunts himself.

quote.quote: Keaton used to say: "Never do a crazy scene with something that isn't real." He was always intensely, exaggeratedly true to life.
quote.author: Mel Brooks

did_you_know_list.title: The painful editing process
did_you_know_list.description: The original version ran 42 reels, more than nine hours of film. With the help of a friend, Von Stroheim cut it down to four hours. But the film was taken away from the director and MGM executives cut it to 140 minutes. The editing was done by Joseph Farnham, who, without reading the book or the script, reduced it to 10 reels. The film was released after this edit, and no longer version was made at the time. But in 1999, restorer Rick Schmidlin released a four-hour version of the film, reconstructed from the original production stills and Von Stroheim's shooting script.

did_you_know_list.title: The director's dissatisfaction
did_you_know_list.description: Few people saw the original 9-hour version of the film. After the film was edited by Stroheim and a friend, and finally by MGM, Stroheim was very unhappy with the final version, the one that was released. He called it "a mutilation of my sincere work at the hands of the MGM executives".

did_you_know_list.title: The loss of much of the film
did_you_know_list.description: No copy of the first version was made, and much of the footage not used in the released version was destroyed so that the silver could be extracted from the celluloid. As a result, a large part of the film was lost forever, and the American Film Institute lists it as one of the 10 most important lost films.

did_you_know_list.title: The trouble in Death Valley
did_you_know_list.description: Reaching California's Death Valley took an entire day in several cars and on horseback. On location, water had to be rationed, and temperatures in the middle of the desert in August reached 48 degrees Celsius. The cameras overheated so much that they had to be wrapped in iced towels.

quote.quote: The most important picture ever made in America... At a time when movies were breeding a greed that could no longer be ignored.
quote.author: New York Herald Tribune

did_you_know_list.title: The set designer
did_you_know_list.description: Ben Carré was brought in to design the sets. He had already worked at the Paris Opera House, and had also lived in California scouting locations for films, which gave him experience.

did_you_know_list.title: Argument among the crew
did_you_know_list.description: Edward Sedgwick directed some scenes after director Rupert Julian walked off the set following a heated argument with the crew and cast.

did_you_know_list.title: The film's many colors
did_you_know_list.description: Several sequences were shot in various color processes. Technicolor was used for the Faust and Bal Masqué scenes, Prizmacolor sequences were shot for the introduction, and Handschiegl (a process that uses stencils for coloring) elsewhere. Only the Technicolor Bal Masqué sequence survived.

did_you_know_list.title: Odessa Steps
did_you_know_list.description: The famous Odessa Steps sequence was not in the original screenplay of Battleship Potemkin, having been added to the film during production

did_you_know_list.title: Many versions
did_you_know_list.description: There are several different editions of Battleship Potemkin, with scenes cut from the original version or with the film's scenes rearranged throughout its running time.

quote.quote: Its virtuosity remains dazzling and is at the service of a revolutionary fervor that can still be experienced.
quote.author: Philip French, critic

did_you_know_list.title: Great Scenes
did_you_know_list.description: The film brings together some of cinema's most memorable scenes, such as the famous dance of the rolls, or the one showing the hallucination of the prospector "Big Jim" who, delirious with hunger, sees "the Tramp" transformed into a chicken. The most celebrated, however, is the one where "the Tramp" cooks his boots: with the airs of a gourmet, the character turns the laces into delicious spaghetti, the soles into a fine, tasty game bird, and the nails into its delicate little bones.

did_you_know_list.title: The boot scene
did_you_know_list.description: "The Tramp" and his scene partner really did eat the boots, which were made of licorice by a confectioner hired especially for the task. A perfectionist, Chaplin shot dozens of takes and had more than twenty pairs of boots come out of the oven before the scene was approved.

did_you_know_list.title: Georgia
did_you_know_list.description: The character "Georgia" was written by Chaplin especially for his new wife, Lita Grey, who later had to give up the role because she became pregnant.

did_you_know_list.title: The two versions
did_you_know_list.description: There are two versions of The Gold Rush, the first from 1925 and the other from 1942. The silent version runs 82 minutes, while the sound version runs 74 minutes.

did_you_know_list.title: 2,500 homeless men
did_you_know_list.description: The 2,500 men playing prospectors were actually homeless men who agreed to be in the film in exchange for a day's wages.

quote.quote: Behind all this - the funny clothes, the mustache and the big feet - I would like to produce something that moves people.
quote.author: Charlie Chaplin

did_you_know_list.title: A lost version
did_you_know_list.description: The first version of Metropolis ran more than three hours, but it was lost

did_you_know_list.title: An expensive film
did_you_know_list.description: It was one of the most expensive films in the history of cinema, costing five million marks at the time, and it nearly bankrupted Universum Film AG;

did_you_know_list.title: Inspiration

did_you_know_list.title: C-3PO
did_you_know_list.description: The android C-3PO from George Lucas's "Star Wars" saga had its look inspired by the gynoid.

quote.quote: A robot's suit over human skin produces a greater thrill than anyone could wish for.
quote.author: Iris Barry

movies.title: Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans

did_you_know_list.title: Camilla Horn out of the film
did_you_know_list.description: Director F.W. Murnau wanted Camilla Horn (with whom he had already worked in Germany on Faust) to play the wife, but she was under contract to the German studio UFA at the time and they refused to let her take part in the film, so the role went to Janet Gaynor.

did_you_know_list.title: One of the greatest films of all time
did_you_know_list.description: In 2007, the American Film Institute named it the 82nd greatest film of all time. It was the first time this film made the list.

quote.quote: With Sunrise, the motion picture camera - for so long heavy and primitive - finally learned to fly.
quote.author: Todd Ludy, critic

did_you_know_list.title: Fire during filming
did_you_know_list.description: The final battle scene sparked a small forest fire near the river. Buster Keaton and the whole crew had to stop filming to fight the fire.

did_you_know_list.title: The real General
did_you_know_list.description: Buster Keaton wanted to use the real General locomotive, which was in Nashville, and the railroad company initially allowed him to use it. However, when it learned that the film was a comedy, the railroad withdrew its permission, and Keaton had to look for a train elsewhere.

did_you_know_list.title: A surprise for Marion
did_you_know_list.description: In the scene where Johnny and Annabelle fill the train's water tank, Marion Mack said in an interview years later that she had no idea she was going to get soaked. Buster Keaton didn't tell her it would happen, so that the actress's shock would be completely genuine.

quote.quote: No other comedian could do so much with the deadpan.
quote.author: James Agee, critic

movies.title: October (Ten Days that Shook the World)

quote.quote: How I wish I had made such a mighty failure.
quote.author: Vsevolod Pudovkin

did_you_know_list.title: Warner Brother
did_you_know_list.description: Sam Warner, the Warner Brother who was nicknamed the "Father of the Talkies" because he insisted that Al Jolson's speech be included in the film, died on Wednesday, October 5, 1927, just one day before the film premiered for the remaining cast and crew.

did_you_know_list.title: You ain't heard nothin' yet
did_you_know_list.description: Al Jolson's (as Jack Robin) famous line "You ain't heard nothin' yet." was an ad-lib. The intention was for the film to synchronize only the music, not the dialogue, but Jolson delivered that line after the song "Dirty Hands, Dirty Face" and the director wisely left it in.

did_you_know_list.title: Names considered
did_you_know_list.description: George Jessel, star of the stage version, was invited to play the same role in the film but turned it down over a salary dispute. Eddie Cantor was also offered the role, and he too turned it down.

block_special.description:
The austere Danish master Carl Theodor Dreyer made The Passion of Joan of Arc more than 80 years ago, yet few would deny that his meticulous production still represents a standard of excellence for any character study in cinema.

The film presents the martyrdom of this blend of warrior and maiden, who carries the weight of a nation on her back and does so through an unshakable faith made evident in the expressive power of the protagonist's eyes. This is largely due to the anguished, ethereal performance of the enigmatic Maria Falconetti (1892-1946), a stage actress Dreyer discovered in Paris. (This was not her film debut, however - and, perhaps discouraged by Dreyer's methods, she never made another film.) Falconetti had her suffering, which is palpable on screen, perversely refined, being forced - legend has it - to kneel on stones and to watch the dailies exhaustively until she knew every feature of her face in detail.

Setting the film in the city of Rouen in 1431 and drawing on the manuscripts of Joan's trial, Dreyer works from a palette of raw emotions: Falconetti's expressions proclaim, loud and clear, her character's present agony, past glories and future fears. Often, by framing Joan's face in close-up and at a slightly skewed angle, he sets her sorrow against the monstrous faces of the judges and theologians gathered to force her confession, creating a claustrophobic, desperate atmosphere out of a simple camera movement.

As in later films, among them Vredens dag (Day of Wrath, 1943) and Ordet (1955), Dreyer addresses questions of faith and spirituality by portraying characters who supposedly have reached a state of grace but are judged by a society of skeptics and violent fanatics. The film remains a fascinating anomaly in the history of European cinema.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by David Jenkins, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

did_you_know_list.title: Film rediscovered after half a century
did_you_know_list.description: A copy of the original version, which had been lost for half a century, was rediscovered in the 1980s in a mental hospital in Oslo, Norway. Other copies were destroyed when the warehouse where they were stored caught fire.

did_you_know_list.title: Real blood
did_you_know_list.description: Real blood from a wound was used in the scene where Joan's arm is cut, but the blood belonged to a stand-in, not Falconetti.

did_you_know_list.title: No makeup
did_you_know_list.description: None of the actors wore makeup, which was unthinkable at the time. Dreyer felt that the camera lens flattered the actors' faces.

quote.quote: Renée Falconetti's Joan of Arc may be the finest performance ever recorded on film.

block_special.description:
Tod Browning's Freaks, one of the most shocking and bizarre films ever produced by a major Hollywood studio, fires in two radically different directions at once. It is both an openly exploitative film (advertised as "the most startling horror story of the abnormal and unwanted") and a work that treats its deformed protagonists with considerable sensitivity. MGM's intention was clear from the start: "I want something that out-horrors Frankenstein," studio executive Irving Thalberg reportedly told the filmmakers, aware of the success Universal had just had with its film.

Browning had directed Dracula for Universal and, although he had a morbid and strange sensibility, he had a strong, clear bond of empathy with his characters. MGM's biggest stars wanted nothing to do with a film like this. Myrna Loy (1905-1983), originally cast as Cleopatra, the trapeze artist, begged the studio bosses to release her from the role. She was replaced by Olga Baclanova (1893-1974).

The action takes place in a traveling circus full of clowns, acrobats and "freaks". Hans (Harry Earles), an elegant little person, has just inherited a fortune. Cleopatra tries to ruin his relationship with his fiancée Frieda (Daisy Earles), while having an affair with Hercules (Henry Victor), the troupe's strongman. She tries to poison Hans, but is caught in the act - and the freaks carry out a terrible revenge.

After a few disastrous preview screenings, it was heavily edited. Even so, it was received with hostility. It was only with the arrival of the 1960s and the counterculture era that it reached its current cult status.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Geoffrey Macnab, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

block_special.description:
Citizen Kane, the directorial debut of Orson Welles (1915-1985), has always been considered "the greatest film of all time", which makes it hard to assess clearly. Myths have formed around it: that Welles pioneered a series of innovative filmmaking techniques, and that the film was dismissed on its release for being considered too pretentious.

Welles was not the first to use techniques such as greater depth of field, sets with visible ceilings, overlapping sound, jump cuts, "naturalistic" dialogue in which lines trample over one another, chiaroscuro lighting, or a narrative with multiple points of view - although no other filmmaker had dared to combine them with as much fervor and aesthetic creativity as he did.

When Citizen Kane opened, most critics received it enthusiastically, but its release was sabotaged. Press baron William Randolph Hearst had no trouble at all recognizing himself in the character of Charles Foster Kane. In the blink of an eye, his entire powerful public relations machine went into action against Welles's film, making sure it never got a decent release.

For such a revolutionary work, the message behind the film is surprisingly conventional: the rich are not to be envied for their wealth, because they have lost the simple pleasures of true love and happiness. Even so, it deserves its top status, first, because Welles's signature is so captivating, stamped so indelibly on every frame, and second, because today viewers can recognize much of Welles in the protagonist himself.

Citizen Kane is still a hugely important film, but amid its visual grandiloquence, its baroque showmanship and its ostentatious techniques - however fascinating they may be - we can hear, like a terrible premonition, the howl of frustration and creative blockage that the future held in store for the brilliant Welles.
block_special.credits: Original review by Phillip Kemp, adapted from the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

block_special.description:
Regarded as the spark of an aesthetic revolution in cinema, Rossellini's Roma città aperta (Rome, Open City, 1945) was the first great work of Italian Neorealism, and it managed to shatter the conventions of the "white telephone" films of Mussolini's regime, which were in vogue in Italy in the early 1940s. Rossellini's film about the Italian Resistance was written during the underground struggle against the Nazis. Recalling Eisenstein's formula of the "choral film", it tells the story of a group of patriots hiding in the apartment of a lithographer named Francesco (Francesco Grand Jaquet). The communist who leads the group, Manfredi (Marcello Pagliero), is hunted by the Gestapo and eventually captured and executed. Pina (Anna Magnani), Francesco's wife, and Don Pietro (Aldo Fabrizi), a good-natured priest, die trying to help Manfredi escape. Yet it is the solidarity of Rome as a city that foreshadows the final victory over the invaders.

The scarcity of technical and financial resources turned out to be a virtue of Rome, Open City, which was shot in a documentary style. By showing real people in real locations, the film brought a breath of fresh air to Western cinema. The freedom of the camera's movements and the authenticity of the characters, combined with a new way of telling a story, were among the qualities that made the film the revelation of the 1946 Cannes Film Festival, where it received the Palme d'Or. Neorealism soon became the aesthetic model for directors interested in a vivid depiction of history and society.

One of the most striking aspects of the film is Rossellini's approach to each character's drama. Some of the film's heroes will remain forever in viewers' hearts. Who could forget the sight of the pregnant Pina running through the bullets, or of the good priest shot before the terrified eyes of the children? Although it may lean toward melodrama, the story is as moving today as it was then. It is no surprise that, after this role, Magnani became one of the greatest actresses in Italian cinema.
block_special.credits: Original review by Dana Duna, adapted from the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

block_special.description:
Akira Kurosawa is the best-known Japanese director in the world. Seven Samurai, a thrilling and humane epic, is his most enduringly popular masterpiece and also his most watched film. The electrifying, if less profound, Hollywood remake The Magnificent Seven (1960) is the most successful of the many Westerns based on Kurosawa's work - including The Outrage (1964), a reworking of Rashomon (1950), and the seminal spaghetti Western Per un pugno di dollari (A Fistful of Dollars, 1964), which Sergio Leone (1929-1989) lifted wholesale from Yojimbo (1961).

This enjoyable cultural exchange is delightful proof of cinema's universal language and appeal. Kurosawa drew inspiration from John Ford's Westerns and made something that boldly breaks with the limited traditions of the typical Japanese jidaigeki - a period film emphasizing sword fights in a medieval Japan portrayed as a fantasy land. Seven Samurai is packed with astonishing action scenes, comic incidents, misadventures, social drama, great character development and the conflict between duty and desire, all handled with impeccable attention to realism.

The film is light, nimble and economical, doing away with unnecessary explanations. It evokes mystery and sustains a mood of apprehension - with brief shots and quick cuts making up the peasants' search for potential protectors and their pleading of their case to Kambei. There are many scenes of overwhelming visual and emotional power - a dying woman dragging herself out of a burning mill and handing her baby to Kikuchiyo, who sits in the stream in shock, sobbing and crying out: "This baby is me. The same thing happened to me", as the blazing mill wheel turns behind him. Yet the film's finest moment is its ending: the three survivors gaze at their comrades' graves while the peasants below, oblivious, turn all their attention to the joyful ritual of planting rice.
block_special.credits: Original review by Angela Errigo, adapted from the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

block_special.description:
The image of a black-cloaked, white-faced Death (Bengt Ekerot) playing chess on the beach with a weary, questioning crusader (Max von Sydow) is as ingrained in the collective memory of film lovers as King Kong atop the Empire State Building. This scene from the Swedish gem The Seventh Seal sums up the importance, the allure and the impact that new forms of cinema had at a certain time when Hollywood's certainties were at a low ebb.

But it is a shame that this scene has come to stand for the whole film in the popular imagination. There is an unfair notion that writer and screenwriter Ingmar Bergman was too solemn in trying to make something that could be an archetype of seriousness and artistic quality. In fact, The Seventh Seal, although rooted in the great themes of Bergman's peak, is a very entertaining, often comic film - a medieval fable influenced by the director's enthusiasm for Akira Kurosawa's samurai films - as concerned with celebrating simple pleasures as with pointing out complex torments.

The knight, constantly tormented by questions about God and nothingness (he even approaches a condemned witch to ask her what the Devil knows about God), represents one side of Bergman. The simple circus performer, gently chided by his practical wife ("You and your dreams and visions", she says in the film's last line), represents the other. He seeks redemption through honest entertainment and is dismayed when his innocent performance is overshadowed by the grotesque, Church-approved spectacle of a crowd of penitents being whipped and tortured. Bergman is outraged and saddened by the evil men do, especially when it is sanctioned by a supposed religion, but the film also celebrates physical and spiritual love, collective artistic expression, food and drink, and natural beauty.
block_special.credits: Original review by Kim Newman, adapted from the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

block_special.description:
A remake of a silent epic released in 1925, Ben-Hur was part of a series of spectacular films that were huge box office hits in the 1950s. After Quo Vadis (1951), The Robe (1953) and The Ten Commandments (1956), Ben-Hur was hailed as the greatest epic of all epics. But it is also remembered for a sarcastic quip ("Loved Ben. Hated Hur") as much as for its achievements. What prompted the criticism was that director William Wyler adopted the theory of Cecil B. DeMille (1881-1959) that audiences of biblical films allowed themselves to enjoy orgies and violence only because, in the end, divine wrath fell upon the wicked.

A more sophisticated filmmaker than DeMille, Wyler felt that it was not enough to bring the temple down on the villains. So the strong, simple story of Judah Ben-Hur (Charlton Heston), the noble Jew betrayed and enslaved by his false Roman friend Messala (Stephen Boyd), alternates crowd-pleasing action scenes with "inspirational" encounters with Christ, which allow Heston to deal with religious matters. Subsequent sword-and-sandal epics, from Spartacus (1960) to Gladiator (2000), toned down the preaching and turned up the violence, suggesting that a lesson had been learned. Still, while Heston and Boyd shine on their chariots, audiences can't help loving Ben-Hur. The film was the biggest commercial hit of the year and held the record for Oscars until Titanic (1997).

block_special.description:
By the mid-1960s, Hollywood had grown tired of Westerns, which were increasingly seen as a relic of another era. Naturally, the films remained essential to understanding the history of cinema, but the times were changing and the genre no longer seemed to have a place in popular culture. Sergio Leone thought otherwise. The Italian director sensed that the dying genre was ripe for reinvention. The lasting influence of his so-called spaghetti Westerns (nicknamed for their Italian locations and their copious use of blood) shows that he was right.

Leone had made a handful of films before inviting the relatively unknown Clint Eastwood to Italy for a remake of Akira Kurosawa's Yojimbo (1961), itself based on Dashiell Hammett's Red Harvest. A Fistful of Dollars (1964) was the first of the iconic Westerns starring the "Man with No Name". Made on a minimal budget, this innovative and refined film became a huge hit, and Leone followed it with For a Few Dollars More (1965), again starring Eastwood as another laconic, anonymous antihero. But the third part of the "Man with No Name" trilogy, The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, is the work that confirmed Leone's reputation as a film legend.

Leone is not terribly interested in plot - in The Good, the Bad and the Ugly he is concerned with purely cinematic elements. He carefully composes every widescreen image as if he were painting a vast landscape; he indulges in extreme close-ups that often reveal little more than a character's eyes. Then there are his radical editing techniques, set to the rhythm of Ennio Morricone's famous score, which places unusual instruments and electric guitars alongside traditional orchestration. Every frame is coated in style the way sweat permanently coats the stars' faces.

The Good, the Bad and the Ugly literally ends on the faces of Eastwood, Wallach and Van Cleef, as the antagonists stage a three-way duel in a cemetery. This scene has become one of the most imitated and parodied in film history. Morricone's hypnotic score builds in intensity while on screen ever-faster cuts move from one face to another, capturing every tense glance, every hand reaching for a gun. Camp, kitsch and exhilarating, the film is the work of a master rewriting the rules of the Western to suit Leone's singular vision.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Joshua Klein, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

block_special.description:
A classic among science fiction adventures that remains as powerful today as when it was first released, Planet of the Apes was a project that had the potential to go terribly wrong. Tim Burton's 2001 remake is an example of everything that could go wrong. Even with the $100 million budget still two decades away, making a film out of Pierre Boulle's book, La Planète des singes remained a risky premise. Having so many actors dressed in ape suits could well have been an invitation for audiences to laugh rather than to be scared.

Before the film went into production, makeup artist John Chambers eased the studio bosses' fears by shooting a test with Charlton Heston (as the human Taylor) and Edward G. Robinson (as the ape Dr. Zaius). Having shown that the ape makeup was convincing, Chambers was given $50,000 to develop the simian effects for the film. Robinson, fearing that hours in the makeup chair would threaten his already fragile health, left the cast and was replaced by Maurice Evans.

It was money well spent. The apes that Taylor and his two fellow astronauts encounter when their spaceship crashes on a desolate planet are genuinely frightening, especially when we and Taylor realize that they are in charge and that humans are mute animals in this strange place. The casting is perfect. Heston, who spends most of the film wearing little more than a leather loincloth, is manly and tough. Roddy McDowall and Kim Hunter, as the "friendly" apes Cornelius and Zira, manage to break free of the confines of their impressive makeup and give moving performances. Punctuated by landmark scenes such as Taylor's first sight of the new planet, his capture and, of course, the unforgettable ending, Rod Serling and Michael Wilson's screenplay is intelligent and packed with sensational dialogue. ("Take your stinking paws off me, you damned dirty ape!"). This classic spawned three sequels, a TV series, the aforementioned disappointing remake and even a hilarious parody in an episode of The Simpsons.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Joshua Klein, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

block_special.description:
An artifact of evident extraterrestrial origin triggers and monitors crucial stages in Man's journey, from ape to star explorer. At the dawn of the age of Man, a mysterious monolith acts as the catalyst for an evolutionary leap among primates, from gatherers and scavengers to armed hunters and killers. Millennia later, a monolith discovered by geologists on duty on the Moon emits alarming shortwave signals in the direction of Jupiter. An expedition to investigate (commanded impassively by Keir Dullea and Gary Lockwood while the specialists sleep in suspended animation) is sabotaged by the spaceship Discovery's computer, HAL (voiced by Douglas Rain), who is psychologically disturbed. Hugely influential yet still unique, coldly detached, obsessive, pretentious, confusing and forever fascinating, 2001 is all of this and more.

It certainly strayed from Stanley Kubrick's stated intention of making a "good, typical science fiction film" out of Arthur C. Clarke's intriguing short story "The Sentinel" (Clarke co-wrote the screenplay). The film defies genre conventions and differs from any science fiction work made before it. Visually, 2001 is undeniably stunning. Groundbreaking special effects, which deservedly won an Oscar, offer an admirable blend of imagination and science. Meticulous mime work and the best makeup available at the time create, in the first of the film's four acts, the most perfect portrayal of apes by human beings ever seen up to that point (and still very effective, although surpassed by John Chambers' creation in Planet of the Apes, 1968). The film is full of unforgettable images: the unexpected and stunning cut from a bone wielded by an ape-man and tossed into the air to a satellite; the alignment of the Sun and the Moon directly on the edge of the monolith; the orbital waltz at the space station and the landing of a spacecraft; the circular habitat of the Discovery crew.

The sound is equally rich, with experimental choral music, classical themes (Richard Strauss's "Also sprach Zarathustra" and Johann Strauss's waltz "The Blue Danube") that are forever associated with the film, and morsels of minimalist dialogue ("Open the pod bay doors, HAL") that have become the source of a wide range of tributes and cultural references.

2001 can be considered a mysterious adventure, a sermon, a vision, but even taken simply as a striking and unsurpassed spectacle, it demands to be seen on a big screen to be appreciated in its full scope. Its weaknesses (excessive abstraction and a deficient narrative built on poorly articulated, unresolved speculation about the origins and destiny of human life) are more than compensated for by the gripping relationship between man and machine, its visual austerity and serenity and, above all, its rhapsodic exaltation of the sky, the Earth and the infinite.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Angela Errigo, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

block_special.description:
Critic Peter Rist called King Hu "the least appreciated of the 'great directors' in the history of cinema" and "one of the most original filmmakers of the 1960s". Hu was the master of wuxia, or martial arts, a genre and tradition that dates back in Chinese cinema to the silent films, but that truly took on its modern form after Hu and some of his contemporaries infused it with a new sophistication in the late 1960s.

Hu took three years to make A Touch of Zen, which is often cited as his masterpiece, in which he fused Chinese history and Buddhist theology with choreographed action and elegant camera movement. He directs with great skill, and the way he uses the camera, with tracking shots and cranes, sometimes reminiscent of Kenji Mizoguchi (1898-1956), is inventive throughout. Working in Taiwan rather than in Hong Kong, where he had made his first wuxia film, Da zui xia (Come Drink with Me, 1966), he makes the most of the dazzling mountain landscapes, which provide a dramatic backdrop.

The action scenes are certainly memorable, but the film is notable for its slow build-up, with the first third consisting of hints and foreshadowing rather than explicit violence. There is also a dose of understated humor. Unfortunately, the time and care Hu lavished on the film were not rewarded with immediate commercial success. Its length led to it being shown in two parts in Taiwan and cut by distributors in Hong Kong. In 1975, this final version won a special technical prize at Cannes and, in 2005, A Touch of Zen was ranked ninth on the Hong Kong Film Awards' list of the Best 100 Chinese Motion Pictures.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Alexander Jacoby, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die.

block_special.description:
"He's a cool, tough guy. A Black private detective, a sex machine with all the ladies. He takes orders from nobody, Black or white, but he'd risk his own neck for his brother. I'm talking about Shaft. Got it?" These lines, from the theme song by Oscar winner Isaac Hayes (1942-2008), are the perfect introduction to the Black American hero/rebel idol John Shaft, played by Richard Roundtree, the title star of the hugely successful feature directed by Gordon Parks. Shaft followed the path opened by Melvin Van Peebles's Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song (1971) and is widely recognized as the film that launched the short-lived (but fondly remembered) explosion of blaxploitation cinema.

The screenplay was written by Ernest Tidyman (1928-1984), author of a popular series of detective stories starring the film's protagonist. After the success of Sweetback, MGM gave Parks - a Black American and a prestigious writer, composer, photographer and film director - permission to make a project aimed at tapping into the emerging Black audience market. Parks wanted a new face for the lead role and found exactly what he was looking for in Roundtree, a former Ebony model and occasional stage actor whose physical presence and acting style had the exact combination of machismo, virility and confidence the role required.

If ever there was a film in which the narrative is simply a vehicle for showcasing a character, it is Shaft. Together, Tidyman, Parks and Roundtree created a strong Black protagonist who - for the first time in Hollywood films - makes his own rules, listens to no one, gives orders instead of taking them and has no qualms about making jokes at the expense of white authorities. Despite (or possibly because of) its subversive and militant undertones, Shaft was extremely profitable among both Black and white audiences, grossing more than 23 million dollars in the United States alone. Such broad success can be partly explained by the fact that Shaft is perfectly at ease in any situation, with all kinds of people, and that his magnetism and his cool under fire transcend any color line.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Steven Jay Schneider, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

block_special.description:
"This film is dedicated to all the brothers and sisters who have had enough of the Man." With the 70,000 dollars he earned for his 1970 comedy Watermelon Man (1970), plus additional funds (including a loan from Bill Cosby), Melvin Van Peebles (b. 1932) - one of the first Black American directors to work in Hollywood - financed his new project, Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song. He wrote, directed, scored and starred in the film, which was a wise economic decision and also ensured his total creative control over the production. In early 1971, Sweetback opened in the only two theaters willing to show it. By the end of that year, the film had become the most profitable independent production in history. A hit across the United States, it grossed more than 15 million dollars.

Sweetback is so original in concept and execution that it defied all expectations, offering a popular alternative to the dominant Hollywood paradigm. But it also borrows narrative themes and conventions from a variety of genres, including gangster chase films, biker films and soft-core porn. Ultimately, Sweetback is a film whose unexpected commercial success secured it a place at the forefront of an explosion of productions aimed at the Black market, with Black casts and/or Black directors - a movement that soon became known by the ambivalent name of blaxploitation.

The shocking opening scene shows us a preteen Sweetback (played by Mario, Melvin's son) working in a brothel, where a grateful prostitute cries out his nickname during an orgasm. We then see an adult Sweetback performing as a porn actor in a sex show in South Central, Los Angeles. After seeing two white police officers beat a young Black activist (Hubert Scales) nearly to death, Sweetback attacks the officers and almost kills them. The rest of the film follows the hero's misadventures: he flees and hitches rides in a desperate effort to avoid capture. At one point, Sweetback's life is threatened by a biker gang, and he survives only by winning a public sexual duel with its female leader. As one reviewer put it, Sweetback "escapes the police by raping a Black woman at knifepoint, impales a policeman with a pool cue, kills several dogs that are following him, heals himself with his own urine and bites the head off a lizard before fleeing across the Mexican border into the desert." The film ends with the words "A 'Baadasssss' Black man is coming back to collect some dues" flashing across the screen.

Whatever one concludes about Sweetback's sociopolitical message, the energy and innovative directing style of Van Peebles can hardly be denied. Making creative use of techniques such as montage, superimposition, freeze frames, jump cuts, zoom-ins, split screen, stylized dialogue, multiple exposure and a great soundtrack, Van Peebles broke new ground and challenged viewers of all races.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Steven Jay Schneider , published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die.

block_special.description:
Bob Fosse's masterpiece is a cynical critique of the last decadent days of the Weimar Republic, on the eve of the rise of National Socialism, with frivolous, catchy songs that mask the troubling events unfolding in Europe.

Brian (Michael York) arrives in Berlin in 1931. He meets Sally Bowles (Liza Minnelli) and the two become lovers. She works at the Kit Kat Klub (note the three Ks), an underground cabaret cut off from the outside world. Sally and Brian's fleeting affair is put into perspective by the violent turmoil surrounding them, which begins to destroy the freedoms they cherish so much.

Glimpses of Nazi brutality go unnoticed by those enjoying themselves at the cabaret. The songs bring the plot and characters to life, driving the narrative while also commenting on the unfolding events. "Maybe This Time" expresses Sally's high hopes; "If You Could See Her" is a terrifying allegory of the intense persecution of Berlin's Jewish population. The songs are performed on the stage of the Kit Kat Klub and, apart from the expressionist angles revealing morally gray spectators, the numbers are staged realistically. Fosse shows the performances from a distance, using the glare of the lights to emphasize the small stage and the silhouettes of heads in the audience - conspirators in this dark world.

The final frames repeat the opening scene, with the smeared glass reflecting those who have finally taken over the audience, identifiable only by their swastika-adorned armbands. A mirror is held up to society, and the figures in it are hazy, distorted, sharing a cruel worldview.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Simon Ward, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie

block_special.description:
The youngest son, Michael Corleone (Al Pacino), returns from World War II outside the family business: organized crime. When his father, Don Corleone (Marlon Brando), is gunned down, however, Michael is driven to carry out a vendetta, a retaliatory killing, bound by blood and "honor" to a violent chain of events of power and survival in the underworld. Ultimately, Michael inherits the role of head of the family, shutting the door on his uncomprehending non-Italian wife (Diane Keaton) as he receives homage as the new "Godfather," or boss.

The film's dialogue and characters immediately entered the collective imagination of moviegoers. Al Pacino (b. 1940) and James Caan (b. 1940) (the hotheaded older brother Sonny) became stars, and the film won the Oscars for Best Picture and Best Screenplay, as well as Best Actor for Brando, in a triumphant comeback. In adapting Mario Puzo's bestseller, Francis Ford Coppola made a gangster opera in the pulp fiction style, an epic about patriarchy, family and America itself. Protests of defamation from Italian Americans were swept aside by the film's immense popularity. Every descendant of immigrants looked on with nostalgia at the Corleone clan making pasta, celebrating and grieving together. The anecdotes, footnotes and postscripts are now part of the folklore - Brando didn't stuff his cheeks with cotton but wore resin pads attached to his molars, and he sent a fake Native American, "Sacheen Littlefeather," to the Oscars ceremony to decline his award.

Coppola set many of the rules of the game for 1970s cinema with his technical mastery. The audacious, visceral and grandiose set pieces are now legendary - the horse's head in the bed, the slaughter of Sonny, the scenes cutting between a sunny garden wedding party and Don Corleone's entourage inside the house, and the stunning finale with murders being carried out during the baptism of the new Corleone (in effect, the rites of consecration for Michael as he assumes the role of the new boss). The film's best qualities reveal Coppola's fluency in the classics, in pulp, film noir and social dramas, but a persistent criticism of The Godfather is that it glorifies the Mafia. Pacino's Michael is the film's hero, and Michael is not a good guy. Even so, its mythic exploration of family ties, even when they are cursed by blood and ambition, keeps drawing viewers in with the idea that having a family (even a Mafia one) is still better than having no family at all.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Angela Errigo, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

movies.title: The Bitter Tears of Petra von Kant

block_special.description:
Having established his credentials as an action-movie superstar with low-budget Hong Kong productions such as Fist of Fury and The Big Boss, Bruce Lee, a cha-cha champion (as well as a karate and kung fu champion), only got the chance to complete one film made to Hollywood production standards. Lee, a martial artist whose physical skills reached a spiritual level, invades (along with his allies John Saxon and Jim Kelly) the island lair of a master villain and disposes of hordes of second-tier henchmen (including Jackie Chan, who gets his neck broken in a quick scene).

Director Robert Clouse (1928-1997) has just the style you would expect from someone directing a Brock Landers adventure (heavy use of zooms and lens flares), and Lee, whose real-life Hong Kong English was heavily accented but fluent and distinctive, is stuck with "Charlie Chan dialogue" consisting of wise, cryptic pronouncements. The action remains formidable, however, since, without the help of wires or the effects used in recent films such as Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, Lee magnificently executes his moves, wielding his signature nunchucks and flexing his oiled torso.

Influential on an entire genre of martial arts films that followed, and also a template for every "fighting" video game, Enter the Dragon earns its place in film history purely through Lee's charismatic presence and its inimitable fight sequences.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Kim Newman, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die.

block_special.description:
This film, the first blockbuster in the history of horror cinema, had an enormous influence on the future of the genre. Never before had a horror film been the object of so much attention prior to its release, so much gossip about conflicts during post-production, so much speculation about why people of all ages stood in line for hours to see a work supposedly capable of inducing fits of vomiting, fainting, and even temporary psychosis. It is hard to convey the true cultural impact of The Exorcist. The film stole headlines from the Watergate scandal, at least for a while caused a considerable rise in the number of "real" cases of demonic possession and, as one critic wrote, "established grossness as a form of mass entertainment".

Inspired by newspaper reports about a 13-year-old Maryland boy whose body had supposedly been possessed by demonic forces, novelist William Peter Blatty turned the possessed boy into a girl. Blatty embellished many details, adding heavy doses of philosophical and theological speculation about the nature of evil, and the result was the 1971 book The Exorcist. Anticipating a bestseller, Warner Bros. bought the film rights, and after several revisions of the original screenplay, Blatty finally produced a version of The Exorcist that lived up to Friedkin's exacting standards.

In an era of student protests, experimental drug use, and the questioning of authority, The Exorcist let viewers revel in the horrific punishments inflicted on the rebellious Regan. But by making demon-Regan so fascinating to watch, so full of indecent surprises, The Exorcist also gave the audience the pleasure of rebellion. The film not only spawned a series of inferior sequels, imitations, and variations on the theme of possession, but also made children with evil powers a dominant theme in horror cinema.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Steven Jay Schneider, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

movies.original_title: Bring Me the Head of Alfredo Garcia

block_special.description:
Richard O'Brien's offbeat stage musical, adapted for the screen in 1975, was a flop on its release. However, when a New York theater began showing it at midnight screenings, word quickly spread about the bizarre science fiction and horror spoof. The film became a cult hit and to this day holds the record for the longest theatrical run, having been shown at the same theater in Munich, Germany, every week for more than 27 years.

A very young Susan Sarandon (b. 1946) and Barry Bostwick (b. 1945) star as Janet and Brad, an innocent couple whose car breaks down on a stormy night, forcing them to seek shelter in a nearby castle, unaware that it belongs to the stockings-and-garters-clad transvestite Frank N. Furter (Tim Curry, reprising his stage role) and his friends from Transylvania, including the sinister Riff Raff (Richard O'Brien) and Magenta (Patricia Quinn). Also living in the mansion are the biker Eddie (Meat Loaf), a failed creation (in the style of Frankenstein's monster) of Frank N. Furter, and Rocky (Peter Hinwood), his perfectly tanned replacement/upgrade.

Narrated by Dr. Everett Scott (Jonathan Adams) and driven by glam rock, the film is a celebration of sexuality: Frank N. Furter and his troupe try to seduce the virginal Brad and Janet to the tune of memorable songs such as "Touch-a Touch-a Touch Me", "Sweet Transvestite" and, of course, "Time Warp". The mix of brazen sexuality, ironic quips, outrageous costumes, and double entendres is unlike anything ever done in cinema. It is easy to see why the catchy songs and highly quotable dialogue became such a huge hit with fans, the most enthusiastic of whom dress up as the characters, act out parts of the film during screenings, and bring props to use at specific moments in the film, for example, throwing rice during the wedding scene. The Rocky Horror Picture Show may not be a film for the whole family, but it is still fantastic kitsch fun.

block_special.description:
A project that actor Kirk Douglas (1916-2020) had wanted to make for years (he owned the rights, but by the time the film finally went into production, he felt he was too old to star in it), One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest earned his son, Michael Douglas (b. 1944), his first Oscar, not as an actor but as a producer.

Based on the bestseller by Ken Kesey, written after his experience working at a veterans' hospital in California, the film is set in a state mental institution where the wily nonconformist Randle P. McMurphy (Jack Nicholson) is committed for rehabilitation. Inside the institution, he is kept under the watchful eye of the sadistic Nurse Ratched (Louise Fletcher, in a role turned down by several major Hollywood actresses, including Jane Fonda, Anne Bancroft, Ellen Burstyn, and Faye Dunaway), and he soon stages a rebellion against her with the help of other patients.

A groundbreaking film that Kesey reportedly never wanted to see (he was supposedly irritated that the story was not told from the point of view of Chief Bromden (Will Sampson), as in his book), One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest became part of Oscar history when it became only the second film up to that time to win all five major awards. Each one was deserved: Czech director Milos Forman (1932-2018) created a hypnotic, humanistic film full of eccentric characters (among the actors who made their film debuts are Brad Dourif (b. 1950) and Christopher Lloyd (b. 1938)), and drew one of the best performances of Fletcher's career. Nicholson, naturally, is captivating as McMurphy, imprisoned yet witty and full of life, and the scenes in which he faces off with the despicable Nurse Ratched are the most electrifying in this modern classic of American cinema.
