movies.original_title: Salò o le 120 giornate di Sodoma

block_special.description:
The screenplay of Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom is based on the work of the same title by the Marquis de Sade, who gave his name to the specific form of sexual perversion the film explores. Although the narrative differs from Sade's book in many respects, it still preserves its essence. The Marquis de Sade's project was partly political, aiming to satirize the dominant institutions of his time, above all the Catholic Church. Pasolini was also fervently anticlerical, but he ties Sodom directly to Italian history.

The film is set in Salò, a very short-lived republic where Mussolini established his last stronghold of resistance at the end of World War II. Pasolini was caught up in these events, and his brother was killed in Salò. In Pasolini's fantasy about this episode of the war, four fascist libertines have total power over a group of young, attractive prisoners of both sexes and subject them to a series of sexual tortures and humiliations. These are presented by the director in a series of coldly formal scenes that are curiously devoid of any erotic tension. Nor is there any intention of developing the characters: even the libertines are barely defined in terms of personality and seem to derive no real pleasure from their debauchery, while their victims are essentially anonymous, simply bodies to be abused and penetrated.

Pasolini's intention was to turn the unlimited use of power, taken to the most radical sexual degradation, into a metaphor for fascism itself, seen as a philosophy that worships power as an end in itself. There are other messages, however. One libertine is identified as a bishop and, at one point, two of the victims are subjected to a sort of wedding ceremony, although the consummation is interrupted by the libertines, who place their own bodies between the newlyweds. And, in a particularly notorious scene, a naked young woman is forced to eat excrement; Pasolini always argued that this was a metaphor for mass consumer capitalism and its production of junk food.

The film ends in an orgy of cruelty: the victims are strangled and scalped, tongues are cut out and nipples are burned. It all unfolds to the sound of Carmina Burana, the famous work by Carl Orff that Pasolini also considered fascist music, along with a reading from the Cantos of Ezra Pound, the American poet who supported Mussolini.

The obscenities the film presents have an undeniable power to shock; perhaps most disturbing is that, at this point in his career, Pasolini had at best an ambiguous attitude toward the body and sexuality. If the aim of pornography is to stimulate sexual desire, Sodom would not fit the definition, because its effect and, presumably, its purpose are to generate revulsion. Shortly after this radical and disturbing film was completed, and even before it was released, Pasolini was murdered. His film was persecuted or banned in many countries, and only after several decades did it become available to the general public in England and the United States.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Edward Buscombe, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

block_special.description:
The film that invented the "summer blockbuster", and the first to pass the famous $100 million mark at the box office, was a genuine phenomenon. In the summer of 1975, everyone was talking about Jaws. The film wrecked a generation's swimming habits and launched the career of a talented young director.

The shoot was famously troubled, prolonged by the difficulties of working at sea and by the malfunctioning mechanical predator. Even so, Jaws is a classic example of storytelling, combining horror, adventure and the journey of an outsider hero who must face the community and his own fear of water. The story deals with the disruption to the lives and livelihoods of the residents of the resort town of Amity after a great white shark decides to settle in its waters. When it attacks on the Fourth of July, police chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) heads out to sea aboard the Orca, with the brave Captain Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Matt Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss), to kill Amity's tormentor.

Jaws gave early signs of Spielberg's pure cinematic instinct, from the use of the animal's point of view to heighten suspense to the push-pull shot in which Brody realizes the creature has devoured a boy before his eyes. But the film's success would have been unthinkable without the score by John Williams (b. 1932), built on two menacing notes that serve as the shark's theme, without Verna Fields' editing and without the actors' performances. It was an ad-lib by Roy Scheider that gave Jaws its best line: "You're gonna need a bigger boat".
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Demetrios Matheou, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.original_title: The Man Who Fell to Earth
The Killing of a Chinese Bookie

block_special.description:
"Someday a real rain will come and wash all this scum off the streets". So mutters tormented cab driver Travis Bickle, played with almost furious intensity by Robert De Niro, in the first of his acclaimed leading roles in Martin Scorsese's films. Bickle's job, crisscrossing New York from one end to the other ("anytime, anywhere"), gives him a sleepless view of the city's underbelly, everything that happens in the dark alleys that most people never witness. He ends up so accustomed to the world around him, however, that he feels numb, invisible and, ultimately, powerless.

Taxi Driver's portraits of urban disorder and malaise are as dark and claustrophobic as they come. The film has some elements of film noir (Bickle's voice-over narration, the jazzy score by Bernard Herrmann (1911-1975)) but departs radically from the pattern when it comes to storytelling. Taxi Driver unfolds like a noir told from the perspective of an anonymous stranger standing in front of a murder scene, peering over the police cordon to see the covered body in the street. What is this person thinking? How would they react when confronted with such vivid exposure to violence?

Scorsese, Schrader and De Niro seem to be asking viewers the same thing. Throughout the film, we are forced to observe the city from Bickle's relentlessly isolated perspective, with only a few glimmers of hope carrying us outside his maladjusted mind. He is Dostoevsky's "underground man", who emerges with a gun and a death wish, an antihero who takes justice into his own hands, taking a hands-on approach to cleaning up the city. "Here is a man who won't take it anymore," he announces triumphantly. "A man who stood up against the scum, the sluts, the dogs, the filth, the shit. Here is a man who stood up."

Is this what we want? In an ironic plot twist (of the "the end justifies the means" kind), Bickle ends up hailed as a hero in his own crusade, and it is hard to say whether Bickle's inadvertent triumph is not, in reality, a tragedy. Because the film has so skillfully knocked our moral compass off its axis, we are left struggling desperately in search of impossible answers.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Joshua Klein, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

movies.title: In the Realm of the Senses
Close Encounters of the Third Kind

block_special.description:
No one expected writer-director George Lucas's film to be a hit. The studio bosses were so convinced that the film, "a science fiction Western" whose main cast was unknown (Harrison Ford, Mark Hamill and Carrie Fisher), would flop that they graciously handed Lucas, free of charge, the merchandising rights to any product related to Star Wars. Obviously, they did not expect it to generate 5 sequels, three "prequel" chapters, a spin-off based on the Ewoks, cartoons, computer games, toys, soundtracks, books, huge video and DVD sales, candy, clothing, bedding and even food (and countless parodies, notably three specific Star Wars episodes of the cartoon Family Guy). The film cost $11 million and grossed more than $460 million, but it did not seem to have the potential to become a huge hit.

But Lucas had big dreams. Two decades before computer imagery was used to create fantastic worlds, the visionary director, using ultra-detailed models, clever tricks and well-chosen locations, told the story of another universe. The evil Empire, dominated by Darth Vader (David Prowse, with the voice of James Earl Jones), is in control; the rebel forces are gathering to try to overthrow the tyrants.

Lucas created a mythology that was enthusiastically embraced by people of all ages. Besides giving rise to various creatures from a galaxy far, far away, his good-versus-evil storyline introduced us to people, phrases and concepts that have since become part of the collective consciousness: the Millennium Falcon (Han Solo's spaceship, which Lucas originally imagined looking like a flying hamburger), lightsabers (the sword-like weapon with its distinctive sound), the Imperial stormtroopers ("May the Force be with you") and, of course, the Jedi knights (today such an integral part of our collective unconscious that an internet campaign urging people to answer "Jedi" to a question about religion on a United Kingdom census form was hugely successful).

By bringing Star Wars to life, Lucas managed to create much more than just a film. He created a world, a new style of filmmaking and an unforgettable space opera that has never been surpassed.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Joanna Berry, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

movies.title: Last Chants for a Slow Dance

block_special.description:
No director since Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980) has captured the delicious voyeurism of horror as well as John Carpenter does in Halloween, a film so full of our most primal anxieties that it still defines the genre 20 years later. Indeed, the comparison between Hitchcock and Carpenter is no exaggeration: Halloween is full of Carpenter's tributes to Hitchcock, from the characters' names - Sam Loomis and Tom Doyle, from Psycho (1960) and Rear Window (1954), respectively - to the casting of Jamie Lee Curtis (b. 1958), daughter of Janet Leigh (1927-2004), the unfortunate shower victim of Psycho.

Halloween's plot is quite simple: a masked psychopath, Michael Myers, stabs and strangles his way through a group of teenage friends as they drink beer and chase after sex, until he finally comes up against the film's great pure force, the virginal babysitter Laurie Strode (Curtis). Despite its minimalism, the evident social anxieties of good versus evil in Halloween's plot are left unresolved at the end, a strategy repeated consistently in other slashers ranging from Friday the 13th (1980) to Scream (1996). The intensity of Carpenter and of Debra Hill's (1950–2005) screenplay lies in placing horror in the placid setting of suburban American life, where young people are presumed (or at least were once presumed) to be safe.

Deconstructing the notion of the home as a protected place, Halloween's camerawork invades the fictional town of Haddonfield with a roaming point-of-view shot. The film opens with a brilliant shot showing everything through the eyes of the killer, then six years old. Carpenter builds a purely aesthetic fear, setting Halloween apart from its own tiresomely expository offspring. Throughout the film, someone is always watching, whether predator or prey. As the film unfolds, we find ourselves lurking around corners, behind shoulders, through windows and through cracks in closet doors, waiting for what we believe to be certain death.

The brilliant pacing and excruciatingly long takes keep the adrenaline high as Michael slinks through the shadows, cheating death several times to stalk the smart Laurie. When the film ends, we are left anxiously wondering what separates fact from fiction.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Kathryn Bergeroo, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

block_special.description:
"In space no one can hear you scream." The tagline on the Alien poster was an obvious come-on, but there was plenty of screaming in theaters. Defying the popularity of Star Wars (1977), Ridley Scott (b. 1937) resurrected the cheap genre of scary monsters from outer space, paired it with a meticulous, big-budget look and created a paralyzing science fiction horror film capable of leaving nerves completely frayed.

Dan O'Bannon's sophisticated screenplay owes a great deal to the ingenious 1950s B movie Giant from the Unknown (1958) and follows the "haunted house" formula of The Cat and the Canary (1939) or Ten Little Indians (1965), but set aboard a spaceship and with a much greater gross-out factor.

The Nostromo is a gigantic cargo ship operating in deep space, with a minimal (and far from conventional) crew led by Captain Dallas (Tom Skerritt) that includes the smart Lieutenant Ripley (Sigourney Weaver) and Jones the cat. Responding to a distress call, they discover an abandoned alien ship and strange eggs. As they examine the eggs, a parasite leaps out of one and latches onto Kane's (John Hurt) helmet, infecting him and, a few days later, wreaking terrifying havoc when a baby alien bursts out of his chest during breakfast. The other actors supposedly didn't know what was going to happen, which made their shock and revulsion genuine.

Scott creates a frisson and uses the dark corridors dramatically as the dwindling crew - who apparently never watched a horror film as teenagers - walks straight into the monster's pair of extendable jaws. What raised the anguish to an art form, through Oscar-winning visual effects, was the unparalleled art direction and design, blending organic and metallic patterns, as well as the (only glimpsed) alien designed by the artist H. R. Giger, whose terrible beauty was given an eerie grace by the statuesque Maasai dancer Bolaji Badejo.

Weaver became a star and an icon overnight as the brave survivor Ripley, facing her final battle in nothing but a T-shirt and underwear. She was supposed to end the film naked, to emphasize human fragility in the face of the perfect killing machine, but 20th Century Fox, eager to avoid an "R" rating (restricted for those under 17) in the United States, vetoed the idea. Unusually for a horror franchise, the sequels were handed to directors famous for their distinctive visual styles - James Cameron, David Fincher and Jean-Pierre Jeunet.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Angela Errigo, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die.

block_special.description:
This potential contender for a Golden Turkey Award in the "kitsch" category ended up becoming one of the big hits of 1984, and its enduring popularity has enshrined it as a classic of the genre. The Terminator is a triumph of style over plot, of cleverness over intelligence, and a combination of elements that adds up to more than the sum of its parts. Its circular narrative about the future's attempt to control the past in order to take control of itself, thereby changing the premises of its own state, is familiar to every fan of postwar science fiction literature (Harlan Ellison, Philip K. Dick, and others) and of postwar television series (such as The Outer Limits and Star Trek).

Shortly after completing low-budget special effects for Roger Corman (b. 1926) and John Carpenter (b. 1948), writer-director James Cameron (b. 1954) adopted his mentors' disarming humor to shield himself from objections about the many plot holes. The vision of a bleak, dark, apocalyptic future was fashionable at the time, as attested by Escape from New York (1981), by John Carpenter, Mad Max (1979), by George Miller (b. 1945), Le dernier combat (The Last Battle, 1983), by Luc Besson (b. 1959), and Forbrydelsens Element (The Element of Crime, 1984), by Lars von Trier (b. 1956).

Cameron's assured style (tech noir, as it was called after a nightclub in the film) and his kinetic energy combined with narrative economy keep the viewer distracted from the absurdity of the whole thing. Even Arnold Schwarzenegger, the epitome of bad acting with his cold facial expression, heavy Austrian accent, and body language learned at the same school as Frankenstein's monster, becomes a major triumph for the film. The casting, Cameron admitted to Wired magazine, "shouldn't have worked. The guy is supposed to be an infiltrator, and it's impossible not to spot him immediately in a crowd, unless everyone looked like Arnold". Nevertheless, everyone who has seen this unlikely phenomenon knows most of the film's lines by heart, including Schwarzenegger's peculiar pronunciation. "I'll be back" is probably the most quoted line of all, often used as a catchphrase on radio and television shows.

If The Terminator's ability to engage its audience recalls the fan cult of The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975), its insistent irony points ahead to the jokes of the Scream series (1999-2011), built on generic clichés. The same can be said of the sadistic violence and the heroine's turnaround at the end. Beneath the surface of this cut-and-paste of science fiction elements lies an even less original slasher movie, featuring a (literally) mechanical killer and a tough heroine (Linda Hamilton) who discovers her capacity to fight back and combat evil. The film's appeal, as with all great films, does not come from its supposed originality. It is the way Cameron brings together familiar elements and breathes new life into them that results in such a memorable experience, one that ultimately changed science fiction films in theaters forever.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Michael Tapper, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die.

movies.title: The Time to Live and the Time to Die

block_special.description:
In the 1960s, teen movies had Frankie Avalon (b. 1940), Annette Funicello (b. 1942), lots of sand (and no sex) and upbeat music, while in the 1970s being a teenager essentially meant getting slaughtered in your bed in a string of horror films. But in 1984, writer-director John Hughes revolutionized the genre with Sixteen Candles, which he followed the next year with The Breakfast Club, a film whose great achievement was finally showing teenagers as they really talk and think.

No other film summed up the period better, or became more of a cult favorite among teenagers, than The Breakfast Club. It made Hughes a name to watch closely - he went on to make the excellent Ferris Bueller's Day Off (1986) and the hugely successful Home Alone (1990) - and it brought together a talented group of young actors (just as Francis Ford Coppola's The Outsiders had done two years earlier) whom the media dubbed the "Brat Pack".

Five very different teenagers are suspended and must serve Saturday detention for various reasons. Despite their differences when the day begins, they end up bonding with one another. We have the school jock (Emilio Estevez), the weirdo with too much eyeliner (Ally Sheedy), the stuck-up princess (Molly Ringwald, teen idol and Hughes's muse ever since she starred in Sixteen Candles), the nerd (Anthony Michael Hall) and the rebel (Judd Nelson), all trying to keep themselves entertained under the watchful eye of the complex teacher Mr. Vernon (Paul Gleason).

This film, which relies on a screenplay of witty one-liners rather than on action, works largely thanks to the cast's characterizations as truths are revealed, resentments are voiced and each of them gets a turn to shine. Although copied in films and TV series, it may well be the definitive teen movie, whether for its perfect timing, its sharp performances, its quotable lines or its time-capsule-worthy 1980s soundtrack, which includes the classic "Don't You Forget About Me" by Simple Minds, written for the film.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Joanna Berry, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die.

movies.original_title: Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters

block_special.description:
Writer-director Oliver Stone (b. 1946) was the first Vietnam veteran to get Hollywood backing to make an autobiographical film about the conflict. The Deer Hunter (1978) and Apocalypse Now (1979) had turned the war into subject matter for movies, but it was Platoon that showed the reality of Vietnam to generations who only came of age after the conflict was over.

Chris Taylor (Charlie Sheen), who stands in for Stone, is an idealistic young man who volunteered to serve with the infantry in Vietnam. He feels torn between two "fathers": the gentle, sensitive super-soldier Sergeant Elias (Willem Dafoe), who smokes pot and listens to soul with the Black soldiers, and the sadistic, scar-faced Sergeant Barnes (Tom Berenger), who drinks and listens to country and western with the rednecks. Chris follows the path of other screen soldiers, "becoming a man", but whereas the recruits whipped into shape by John Wayne always ended up saluting the flag, Chris ends up losing faith in his country amid the blood and confusion.

Although it is overly schematic in pitting the two sergeants against each other and contrasting their philosophies, Platoon is a powerful film. Terrifying as he is, Barnes teaches Chris how to survive rather than become a martyr - the climax, unthinkable in earlier films, has Chris shooting one of his own superiors rather than facing the enemy. Harrowing and suspenseful as it is, the film is not devoid of nostalgia - the soundtrack is made up of big 1960s hits and, in one scene, the soldiers sing "The Tracks of My Tears" by Smokey Robinson & The Miracles.
block_special.credits: Summary based on the text by Kim Newman, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

block_special.description:
In one of the first scenes of the 1988 film Who Framed Roger Rabbit, the human protagonist, detective Eddie Valiant, played by Bob Hoskins (b. 1942), is drinking at a bar when he is approached by a local jerk. The guy starts needling Valiant about his choice of clients, asking who he was working for that week: "Goofy? Or Screwy Squirrel?". Valiant kicks his tormentor's stool out from under him. Gripping the man's head in his hands and shaking with rage, he growls: "Get this, meatball: I - don't - work - for - toons!".

But, as you probably know, not only does Valiant work for toons, but the success of Who Framed Roger Rabbit soon made the rest of Hollywood want to work for them too. When that film cast human actors alongside a bunch of rubbery, spring-loaded, violent cartoon characters, it was taking a huge risk: the film went about $28 million over budget, attempting technical feats of animation that had never been done before to make the cartoons and humans look as if they were really shooting and grabbing each other. But it paid off, grossing $156 million and winning three Oscars.

Roger Rabbit was far from the first film to feature cartoons and humans crossing the, well, color line. Cab Calloway (1907-1994) made appearances in Betty Boop cartoons such as Minnie the Moocher (1932), some of which opened with live-action footage of the Cotton Club bandleader dancing before revealing a version of him rotoscoped into an animated ghost. By the 1940s, animation technology was good enough for humans to share the screen with cartoons, so Gene Kelly could tap-dance with Jerry the mouse in Anchors Aweigh (1945). But Roger Rabbit broke new ground, even beyond Jessica Rabbit's curves: it proved to film studios not only that audiences loved human-cartoon mash-ups, but that cartoons in general could make a lot of money.

Imitators followed, and joint cartoon-human productions became a fruitful genre between the late 1980s and the mid-1990s. Like Roger Rabbit, these subsequent productions were tinged with racial messages, the tension (sexual or otherwise) between flesh and blood / pen and ink flickering with the danger and thrill of miscegenation. Toontown is a depraved but lovable ghetto in danger of being razed; in the 1989 music video for Paula Abdul's "Opposites Attract", she sings a duet with a cartoon feline character called MC Skat Kat. "It's no fiction / just a natural fact", they whisper. "We come together / because opposites attract".
block_special.credits: Summary based on the article "When Hollywood Went to Toontown", by Madeline Leung Coleman on topic.com.

reviews.review_description: E Christopher Nolan fez mais uma vez, entregou uma obra-prima que como muitas outras obras, divide opiniões.

A Origem (Inception, 2010) não é nenhuma esfinge. Na verdade, a sua estrutura, emprestada dos filmes-de-assalto, é bem trivial. Acompanhamos o planejamento de um golpe enquanto se aprende o essencial de cada personagem. Na hora de pôr o golpe em prática, termina o ensaio, começam os imprevistos.

Em 2000, Christopher Nolan surpreendeu o mundo ao lançar Amnésia. Seu grande atrativo era a engenhosidade de roteiro e edição, que permitia que a trama fosse contada, literalmente, de trás para frente. Era um exercício de talento de um diretor ainda iniciante e, ao mesmo tempo, um desafio aos espectadores. Uma década depois, Nolan repete a proeza com A Origem. Só que em níveis bem mais ousados.

Lembro-me claramente a primeira, e até recentemente única vez que assisti A Rede Social. Lembro-me de pensar algo assim: “tenho que ver, pois é um filme de David Fincher, mas o assunto – a criação do Facebook – não poderia ser menos interessante para mim”. À época, não usava a ferramenta e mesmo hoje tenho minhas reservas pessoais. De toda forma, tenho a vívida memória de ter saído do cinema totalmente de queixo caído. Essa impressão perdurou ao longo dos anos e, agora, quando finalmente revi o oitavo filme de Fincher para elaborar a presente crítica, ela foi reconfirmada em sua integralidade, talvez até ampliada.
Enquanto o Facebook conecta pessoas, David Fincher isola Mark Zuckerberg em um filme sobre dissonâncias

Sabe aqueles filmes que começam mal pacas? Acredite. A Rede Social começa de forma impecavelmente chata, talvez, para mostrar o quão controversa é a figura de Mark Zuckerberg, criador do Facebook, um fenômeno da internet. Será?
A essa altura do campeonato, muita gente já deve ter visto O Segredo da Cabana (The Cabin in the Woods) e dito pra você: vá assistir sem saber absolutamente nada sobre o filme!

Saí do cinema com uma sensação cada vez mais rara de se ter com a Sétima Arte. Sabem aquela sensação gostosa de ter visto algo diferente, com um fator “uau” gigantesco, daquelas que nos fazem ter vontade de ver tudo novamente, por mais que saibamos que essa sensação não se repetirá em sua plenitude? Sabem também quando nós mergulhamos de tal maneira no filme que, quando os créditos começam a rolar, nós meio que vagarosamente despertamos de um sonho – ou pesadelo, depende da película – e demoramos uns cinco, dez minutos para entendermos o que está acontecendo ao nosso redor?
Suspense espacial de Alfonso Cuarón encanta-se com a fragilidade e a tenacidade humanas

O universo é hostil. Sem oxigênio, sem som, no vácuo, ele não oferece a menor condição de sobrevivência à vida humana caso esteja fora deste planeta azul chamado Terra. As breves visitas do homem neste ambiente inóspito são sempre repletas de aparatos desenvolvidos para garantir sua existência, por mais que eles em muitos casos estejam longe do confortável. Foi exatamente com este cenário em mente, de desconforto e do risco constante, que o diretor Alfonso Cuarón conceituou Gravidade. Um filme que impressiona pela ousadia, tanto de narrativa quanto estética, sem jamais deixar de lado o clima de tensão.

Mesmo com uma filmografia tão curta (apenas 3 filmes), Steve McQueen há muito tempo já mostrou a que veio. Tanto em Fome quanto em Shame, filmes de temáticas tão distintas entre si, o diretor traz em seu estilo seco, cru e realista uma forma de ressaltar as nuances de suas obras, experiências desconfortáveis e difíceis, porém sempre sinceras naquilo que querem retratar. Com 12 Anos de Escravidão não é diferente, com McQueen atingindo seu ponto máximo enquanto realizador.

A saída da sessão para a imprensa e indústria de 12 Anos de Escravidão (12 Years a Slave) no Festival de Toronto era como uma procissão de lamentos. Poucas pessoas conversavam e a maioria enxugava as lágrimas. Algumas seguiam chorando minutos após o fim do filme.

12 Anos de Escravidão chega aos cinemas aproximadamente 126 após a abolição da escravatura no Brasil, que ocorreu com a Lei Áurea de 1888. Os Estados Unidos acabaram com a escravidão algumas décadas antes, em 1863, mas em um processo bem mais conflituoso, que gerou uma guerra que dividiu o país.
